# King's Scholar
The title "King's Scholar" historically refers to scholars who have been granted special privileges and scholarships originally endowed by monarchs at certain prestigious educational institutions in England. The tradition began in 1317 when King Edward II sent boys from his household to study at Cambridge. It was further formalized at Eton College in 1440 by King Henry VI, who established Eton as a charity school for "poor, scholarly boys" and increased the number of King's Scholars to 70 in 1443.
At Eton College, King's Scholars (also known as "Collegers" or "tugs") are selected via a competitive examination and become residents of "College," the oldest house at Eton. They are distinguished by wearing a black academic gown and participate in traditions and privileges not extended to other students ("Oppidans"). While a Foundation Scholarship originally covered all fees, in recent years it has become means-tested, and now may be accompanied by fee waivers depending on family circumstances. Notable King's Scholars from Eton include figures in politics, literature, science, and academia such as Boris Johnson, John Maynard Keynes, Kwasi Kwarteng, and Aldous Huxley.
The designation of King's Scholar also exists at institutions such as Westminster School (where they are called King's or Queen's Scholars depending on the monarch) and King's College Cambridge, as well as the seven King's Schools re-founded by Henry VIII. These scholarships recognize academic or musical excellence and often include special privileges such as gown-wearing, cathedral association, and ceremonial rights. The system has evolved at some schools to include Queen's Scholars in recognition of changing gender policies and reigning monarchs.
